canon.title: The European alliances, 1871–1914
canon.about: Classical facts of the alliances and crises of the European powers from the peace of Frankfurt (1871) to the declarations of war of July and August 1914: states as collective beings, with their sovereigns and ministers. It is the classic case of structural balance, whose alliances Antal, Krapivsky and Redner (Physical Review E 72, 036121, 2005) follow; here the signs are coded occasion by occasion from what the states and statesmen do, not chosen to make the network balance. A seed canon, drafted from general knowledge by a language model; every assertion names the standard reference it is to be checked against, and none is checked yet. Its selection is diplomatic history's: the great powers and a few Balkan states, their treaties, crises and wars, and the men who signed; peoples, parliaments, opinion, finance and the colonial world appear only where a treaty or a crisis names them, and the smaller states (Belgium, Romania, Greece, Montenegro) are left out. Signs between states: +1 allied or aligned at the occasion; -1 at war, a peace dictated by the victor, a declared crisis between them, or one the target of the other's treaty (role target). All dates are Gregorian; Russian events, which Russia dated by the Julian calendar until 1918, are given in the Gregorian dates of the Western sources.

sources.cite: Taylor, A. J. P., The Struggle for Mastery in Europe 1848-1918 (Oxford, 1954)
Langer, W. L., European Alliances and Alignments 1871-1890 (New York, 1931)
Langer, W. L., The Diplomacy of Imperialism 1890-1902 (New York, 1935)
Kennan, G. F., The Fateful Alliance: France, Russia, and the Coming of the First World War (New York, 1984)
Kennedy, P. M., The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism 1860-1914 (London, 1980)
Nish, I. H., The Anglo-Japanese Alliance: The Diplomacy of Two Island Empires 1894-1907 (London, 1966)
Clark, C., The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914 (London, 2012)

occasions.label: Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors
The Treaty of Frankfurt: France cedes Alsace and most of Lorraine and pays an indemnity
The three emperors meet in Berlin
The League of the Three Emperors: the Schönbrunn convention of Russia and Austria-Hungary, which Germany joins
The War in Sight crisis: Russia and Britain warn Germany off a war on France; the tsar and Gorchakov in Berlin
occasions.note: Gorchakov's circular that peace was now assured humiliated Bismarck; how far Bismarck meant war is disputed.

occasions.label: Russia declares war on the Ottoman Empire
The Treaty of San Stefano, dictated to the Porte: a great Bulgaria under Russian protection
The Cyprus Convention: Britain guarantees the Porte's Asian lands against Russia and occupies Cyprus
The Congress of Berlin revises San Stefano: Bulgaria cut down, Bosnia to Austria-Hungary's occupation, Serbia independent
Alexander II's angry letter to Wilhelm I, the box on the ears
Wilhelm I meets Alexander II at Alexandrovo and makes peace with him
The Dual Alliance of Germany and Austria-Hungary, secret, against an attack by Russia
occasions.note: Wilhelm I ratified it only after Bismarck threatened to resign.

occasions.label: Alexander II assassinated; Alexander III succeeds
France imposes a protectorate on Tunis, which Italy had wanted
The Three Emperors' Alliance, secret, renewing the league
occasions.note: Giers, then running the foreign ministry for the aged Gorchakov, and Saburov were its Russian authors.

occasions.label: The Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, defensive above all against France
Britain defeats Urabi at Tel el-Kebir and occupies Egypt, an Ottoman province, France having declined to act with it
occasions.note: There was no war with the Porte, which protested and remained nominal suzerain; Egypt divided Britain and France until 1904.

occasions.label: The three emperors meet at Skierniewice, after the league's renewal in March
Serbia attacks Bulgaria and is beaten at Slivnitsa; Austria-Hungary halts the Bulgarian advance
occasions.note: Serbia had been Austria-Hungary's client since their secret treaty of 1881.

occasions.label: Alexander of Battenberg driven from the Bulgarian throne; Russia breaks with Bulgaria, Austria-Hungary resisting Russian control of it
The Triple Alliance renewed, with new promises to Italy
The first Mediterranean Agreement completed: Austria-Hungary adheres to the Anglo-Italian notes of 12 February
The Reinsurance Treaty of Germany and Russia, secret
occasions.note: Signed by Bismarck and Count Pavel Shuvalov.

occasions.label: Bismarck closes the Reichsbank to Russian bonds, the Lombardverbot
The second Mediterranean Agreement of Britain, Austria-Hungary and Italy, against Russian designs on Bulgaria and the Straits, urged on Salisbury by Bismarck
occasions.note: Bismarck's letter to Salisbury of 22 November 1887 is the act of Germany's here.

occasions.label: Wilhelm II succeeds; Bismarck stays chancellor
The first Russian loan floated in Paris
Wilhelm II forces Bismarck out; Caprivi chancellor
The Reinsurance Treaty lapses, Caprivi declining the renewal Giers asks for
The French squadron at Kronstadt, the tsar standing for the Marseillaise; the consultative pact of 27 August
The Franco-Russian military convention signed by the chiefs of staff, against the Triple Alliance
The military convention ratified by an exchange of notes
Bismarck in Berlin, reconciled with Wilhelm II
Caprivi dismissed
Alexander III dies; Nicholas II succeeds
The Triple Intervention: Russia, Germany and France make Japan give back the Liaodong peninsula
The Kruger telegram: Wilhelm II congratulates the Transvaal on repelling the Jameson Raid
Death of Bismarck
Fashoda: Kitchener meets Marchand on the Nile; France gives way
Delcassé in St Petersburg extends the Franco-Russian alliance
Queen Victoria dies, Wilhelm II at her bedside with the new king
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance, aimed at Russia in the Far East
The Triple Alliance renewed
The Prinetti-Barrère exchange: Italy promises France neutrality
occasions.note: The letters are variously dated, June to November 1902. Bülow had spoken in the Reichstag of Italy's extra dances.

occasions.label: Edward VII's visit to Paris
President Loubet and Delcassé in London; Delcassé and Lansdowne open the talks
Japan attacks the Russian fleet at Port Arthur: the Russo-Japanese War
The Entente Cordiale
The Dogger Bank incident: the Russian fleet fires on Hull trawlers; France mediates
Wilhelm II lands at Tangier: the first Moroccan crisis
Delcassé forced to resign under German pressure
Wilhelm II and Nicholas II sign a defensive alliance on the imperial yacht
occasions.note: Never ratified: Russia's ministers voided it, and Bülow offered his resignation over Wilhelm's amendment.

occasions.label: The Treaty of Portsmouth ends the Russo-Japanese War
The Algeciras conference: Germany isolated, with only Austria-Hungary at its side; Grey stands by France and allows military conversations
The Franco-Japanese agreement
The Russo-Japanese convention
The Anglo-Russian Convention on Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet
Edward VII meets Nicholas II at Reval
Edward VII visits Wilhelm II, who refuses any limit to his navy
Izvolsky and Aehrenthal bargain at Buchlau: Bosnia for the Straits
occasions.note: What was agreed is disputed; no minute was kept.

occasions.label: Austria-Hungary annexes Bosnia-Herzegovina
The Daily Telegraph interview, and Bülow's failure to defend the Kaiser before the Reichstag
Austria-Hungary indemnifies the Porte for Bosnia
Germany's démarche makes Russia accept the annexation; Serbia submits
Bülow resigns; Bethmann Hollweg chancellor
Nicholas II visits Edward VII at Cowes
Nicholas II visits Victor Emmanuel III: the secret Russo-Italian agreement of Racconigi
Death of Edward VII
Nicholas II and Sazonov at Potsdam: a German-Russian détente on Persia and the Baghdad railway
The second Moroccan crisis: the Panther at Agadir, the Mansion House speech, the Franco-German settlement
Italy declares war on the Ottoman Empire for Libya
The Serbo-Bulgarian treaty, under Russian patronage
Poincaré, prime minister, in Russia
The First Balkan War: the Porte at war with Serbia and Bulgaria
The Peace of Ouchy: the Porte cedes Libya to Italy
The Grey-Cambon letters: Britain and France to consult if either is threatened
The ambassadors' conference under Grey, to the Treaty of London: Albania made, Serbia kept from the Adriatic
The Second Balkan War: Bulgaria attacks Serbia and Greece, and the Ottomans retake Adrianople
The Treaty of Bucharest, imposed on Bulgaria
Pašić in Vienna sees Berchtold
Austria-Hungary's ultimatum makes Serbia leave northern Albania; Wilhelm II, in Vienna, approves
The Liman von Sanders affair: a German general to command at Constantinople; Russia protests
Wilhelm II visits Franz Ferdinand at Konopischt
Franz Ferdinand and his wife assassinated at Sarajevo
occasions.note: The assassins were Bosnian Serbs armed through Serbian officers of the Black Hand; how much the Serbian government knew is disputed.

occasions.label: The Hoyos mission: Wilhelm II and Bethmann promise Austria-Hungary support against Serbia
occasions.note: Franz Joseph's letter to Wilhelm II, carried by Hoyos from Berchtold's office, made the request.

occasions.label: Poincaré, now president, in St Petersburg with Viviani
Serbia's reply to the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum of 23 July; Austria-Hungary breaks relations; Russia stands by Serbia
Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
occasions.note: Berchtold put before the emperor a report of a Serbian attack at Temes-Kubin, which he struck from the declaration when it proved false.

occasions.label: Russia's general mobilization, ordered by Nicholas II at Sazonov's urging
Germany declares war on Russia
The secret alliance of Germany and the Ottoman Empire, against Russia
Italy declares its neutrality: Austria-Hungary's war is not the defensive case of the Triple Alliance
Grey tells Cambon that the British fleet will protect the French coasts
Germany declares war on France
Britain's ultimatum over Belgium expires: Britain at war with Germany
occasions.note: Bethmann's scrap of paper, to the British ambassador Goschen.

occasions.label: Austria-Hungary declares war on Russia
France and Britain declare war on Austria-Hungary
Japan, Britain's ally, declares war on Germany
After the Ottoman raid on Russia's Black Sea ports, Russia, Britain and France declare war on the Ottoman Empire

ties.note: In 1895 the two acted together against Japan.
Björkö is signed but never ratified, and its +1 is the weakest of these signs; at Algeciras, months later, Russia voted with France.
1887: Bismarck sponsors Britain's agreements with Germany's allies. 1912-13: Grey and the German ambassador work together in the conference.
At Algeciras Italy, still Germany's ally, sided with France on the votes that mattered (-1, the weakest of these signs).
Italy's neutrality is coded -1: it held the alliance void because Austria-Hungary had attacked without consulting it. It went to war on Austria-Hungary in May 1915, beyond this canon.
1906: Austria-Hungary alone voted with Germany. 1908: Britain protested the annexation as a breach of the Treaty of Berlin and backed Russia's call for a conference.
Sarajevo is coded as a crisis between the two states, whatever the Serbian government's part.
1882 is the weakest of these signs: an occupation of the Sultan's province without war on the Sultan.
1878: the Congress makes Serbia independent of the Porte after their war of 1876-78.
Over the Dual Alliance Bismarck won by threatening to resign; the act remembered is the alliance signed.
1894: a reconciliation, not a return to office.
At the declaration Berchtold misinformed the emperor about Temes-Kubin; the sign is that of the act remembered, the war declared together.
Uncle and nephew; 1908 is coded from the quarrel over the navy, the estrangement of the two well attested.
Izvolsky held that Aehrenthal had announced the annexation before the Straits were settled, as he understood their bargain.
